hook: Naga's entire executive career was built inside two companies that run some of the largest real-time systems on Earth, LinkedIn and Uber, rising internally at Uber over eleven years to become CTO of a platform operating across cities, countries, and hundreds of millions of users.
name: Praveen Neppalli Naga

quote.text: Scaling systems is often easier than scaling organizations. Data is more important than models when it comes to AI. Speed and clarity beat perfection in most real-world decisions.
quote.context: Praveen Neppalli Naga, personal LinkedIn profile summary

reading.body:
Praveen Neppalli Naga's entire technical identity is built on operating systems at scale, not designing them in theory, making him one of the few CTOs whose résumé is entirely internal promotions across two of the world's highest-throughput consumer platforms.

The eighteen-year arc from software engineer at LinkedIn in 2008 to company-wide CTO at Uber in 2025 passed through every intermediate layer: engineering manager, senior director, vice president, divisional CTO. That progression matters because each step added organizational surface area alongside technical scope. His five patents in indexing, analytics, and job-matching are consistent with that trajectory, covering infrastructure problems that arise specifically when systems must return results in real time across hundreds of millions of concurrent users. The work is not foundational research but applied engineering at the point where latency and volume collide.

His stated view that data is more important than models in AI reflects the operational context he came from. Uber's core businesses, ride-hailing and delivery, depend on continuous streams of location, demand, and supply data. A model running on stale or incomplete data fails in the field regardless of its architecture. That framing aligns with the site's broader argument that what constrains AI in production is often not the model itself but the infrastructure surrounding it, including the real-time pipelines that feed it. The data here does not cover Uber's compute footprint, power consumption, or data center strategy, so no direct connection to those constraints can be drawn from it.
